newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt can do little to curb property prices-analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK govt can do little to curb property prices-analysts.

text.p: Scarcity plus demand equals value -- and in Hong Kong nothing is as scarce as land.
Rocketing property prices have again grabbed the attention of the crowded colony, cheering investors until the government began hinting of fresh intervention to curb speculators.
But analysts said the fundamentals of a growing population, a recovering economy, stable interest rates and limited land supply meant prices would go up.
"There are limits to the ability of government," said analyst Desmond Cheung of Vickers Ballas. "Even in 1994, the major factor was market forces."

The property market's gradual recovery this year from a slump in 1994-95, partly attributed to a government clampdown on speculators, has been a key factor driving the record run by the stock market, which is about 30 percent weighted in property stocks.
Then weekend reports that a buyer paid HK$1.5 million (US$192,000) just to be first in line to buy a flat in a new luxury development caught the eye of government officials.

Secretary for Housing Dominic Wong said on Monday the government was concerned about speculative activities, especially their possible impact on the end-users' market, and was setting up a task force to look into the situation.
While property stocks were stable on Tuesday, they were no longer at the forefront of the market's advance.
"Investors will be cautious on properties until we see what the government intends to do," said Teresa Wong, chief dealer at DBS Securities.
But with most of a 1994 anti-speculation package still in place, analysts said there was little new that officials could do.

"It's really hard to think of any other new measures except for some rejected ones like a capital gains tax on buying and selling properties and shell companies," said Cheung of Vickers Ballas. "They could further restrict mortgage lending, especially for those luxury flats."
The government took measures to curb property speculation in 1994 after flat prices doubled in a year.

Key measures included restricting forward sales of unfinished flats to not more than nine months before completion and increasing initial deposits to 10 percent from five, raising cost and risk for speculators.

Prices retreated 10 to 30 percent from March 1994, when a package was promised, until the market bottomed out in late 1995. But the slump coincided with rising interest rates, which as much as the government measures, helped drive down prices.
The pre-sale period was relaxed to 12 months in December last year, but the overall package remains intact.
Analysts say prices have caught fire again because people could afford them, first in the mass market and later in the luxury sector.

The flames were further fanned as interest rates stabilised. Banks cut mortgage rates in a battle for market share and developers offered top up loans to get around the ceiling limiting mortgages to 70 percent of a property's value.
Speculation and the sharpest price rises appear to be in the luxury sector, but the mass market is picking up pace as well.
"People are very sentiment (driven) in home buying," said Cheung. "When the market is boring, they may need to buy but they don't decide. They think prices may fall further.
"When the market's bottom is confirmed, and the market is going to rise, no matter whether they are speculator, investor or end-user they all join in."
